issues.description: The authors state that after excluding 64 suffixes that occur in fewer than 20 words, '95 suffixes' remain. However, the arithmetic is wrong: 154 minus 64 equals 90, not 95. This is a straightforward numerical error that raises questions about the accuracy of other reported computations.
issues.quote: we excluded all suffixes that occur in fewer than 20 different words in the CELEX database, i.e. 64 suffixes (Baayen et al., 1993). For the remaining 95 suffixes, the mean diagnosticity and specificity values were virtually unchanged

issues.description: In Experiment 2, the authors report 'for the token analyses - z = 0.60, p < 0.01' for the specificity-by-condition interaction. A z-value of 0.60 yields a two-tailed p-value of approximately 0.55, making p < 0.01 impossible. This is either a transcription error in the z-value or the p-value, but either way it reflects a serious reporting inaccuracy that prevents replication and undermines confidence in the token-based results.
issues.quote: the interaction between specificity and condition was significant, such that the target spelling became used more often in the congruent condition than in the incongruent condition as its specificity increased (B = 1.9, z = 2.8, p < 0.01; for the token analyses - z = 0.60, p < 0.01)

issues.description: Multiple key statistics reported in the Experiment 3 results text differ from values in Table 5. For go-past time, the text reports B = 41 and t = 3.837, while Table 5 shows B = 43 and t = 3.76. For regressions-out, the text reports B = 0.3 and z = 3.12, while Table 5 shows B = 0.25 and z = 2.65. These are not rounding differences—the estimates and test statistics are materially different, suggesting at least one source is reporting from a different model or analysis.
issues.quote: There was an effect of congruency on go-past time (B = 41, t = 3.837, p < 0.001)... The effect of congruency on regressions-out was significant in the expected direction... (B = 0.3, z = 3.12, p < 0.01)

issues.description: Comprehension accuracy is reported as '0.86%' (ranging from '0.66% to 0.98%'). These values are nonsensical as percentages—0.86% would indicate near-chance performance. The values appear to be proportions (0.86, 0.66, 0.98) that have been incorrectly labelled with percent signs, or conversely, should read 86%. Because comprehension checks were used to ensure task engagement, the proper reporting of this metric is essential for evaluating participant compliance.
issues.quote: Average accuracy on comprehension trials was 0.86% (ranging from 0.66% to 0.98%)

issues.description: In Experiments 1 and 2, the models include only a random intercept for subjects (e.g., '(1|subject)'), with no random intercept or slope for items (suffixes or stimuli). This violates the principle of fully crossed random effects (Barr et al., 2013), artificially deflates standard errors by treating items as fixed, and inflates Type I error. Given that suffixes are the primary stimulus variable and only a limited number are used (20 in Experiment 1, 11 in Experiment 2), item variability is especially important to model. Experiment 3 adds random intercepts for suffixes, but inconsistently across experiments.
issues.quote: This analysis was expressed in the model glmer (response ~ condition + (1|subject), data, family = "binomial").

issues.description: The authors explicitly state they had no concrete predictions about which of six eye-tracking measures would show effects, yet they test all six without any correction for multiple comparisons. Finding significance on 2 of 6 tests (33%) under an exploratory framework inflates family-wise Type I error substantially. The effect observed on go-past time and regressions-out may be false positives. The analyses are presented as confirmatory when they are acknowledged to be exploratory.
issues.quote: We did not have any concrete predictions as to which eye-movement measures would be affected by the diagnosticity manipulation, so we chose to monitor a variety of typically studied measures

issues.description: No pre-registration is mentioned anywhere in the manuscript. Given that the authors admit to exploratory analysis of multiple eye-tracking outcomes, use an unspecified set of follow-up analyses across three experiments, and make post-hoc sign transformations of predictor variables, the absence of pre-registration means that researcher degrees of freedom are extensive and undisclosed. The OSF link is cited for data storage only.
issues.quote: Data for all experiments can be found in the OSF storage for this project.

issues.description: To test whether diagnosticity graded participants' category judgements, the authors 'multiplied our diagnosticity measure by -1 for noun-diagnostic suffixes and substituted this measure in our model, in place of the condition variable.' This sign transformation is not pre-specified or theoretically motivated before the results are seen, and the justification (to check whether it was 'not due to the sign-transformation') is itself circular—the separate analyses were conducted because of concerns about the transformation, suggesting it was noticed to be potentially problematic only after results were inspected.
issues.quote: In order to investigate this statistically, we multiplied our diagnosticity measure by -1 for noun-diagnostic suffixes and substituted this measure in our model, in place of the condition variable.

issues.description: The formula for type diagnosticity is stated as: 'dividing the number of words ending in this suffix and falling into this category by the total number of words falling into this category.' As written, the denominator is the total number of words in the lexical category (e.g., all nouns in CELEX), yielding P(suffix|category)—which is specificity-like, not diagnosticity-like. However, the Appendix A values sum to approximately 1 across categories for each suffix (e.g., +ness: A=0.000, N=0.999, V=0.001 ≈ 1), indicating the actual computation is P(category|suffix). The stated formula contradicts the computed values.
issues.quote: type diagnosticity is calculated by dividing the number of words ending in this suffix and falling into this category by the total number of words falling into this category.

issues.description: The authors state that verb suffix fillers in Experiment 3 were not analysed 'because the majority of verb suffixes do not discriminate lexical category (i.e. diagnosticity is less than 0.5).' However, Appendix A shows –ate has Diagnosticity_V = 0.687, –ide has 0.412, and –ize (though not used) has 0.995. Of the 10 listed filler verb suffixes (–ate, –ade, –eer, –le, –yse, –ide, –our, –ice, –ure, –art), several have non-trivial verb diagnosticity. The rationale for exclusion is therefore inconsistent with the supporting appendix data.
issues.quote: Forty filler nonwords whose suffix spellings were diagnostic for verbs were added so that sentence contexts would be balanced across all three lexical categories. These filler nonwords were not analysed, because the majority of verb suffixes do not discriminate lexical category (i.e. diagnosticity is less than 0.5).

issues.description: The authors report that sentences in the congruent and incongruent conditions differ significantly in the number of words preceding the target (congruent: 4.75, incongruent: 5.23, t(64) = 2.07, p < 0.05). More words before the target means more syntactic and semantic context is available in the incongruent condition, which could independently drive longer go-past times and more regressions—the two measures that showed significant congruency effects. No covariate controlling for pre-target length was included in the reported models.
issues.quote: Note that the number of words pre-target was slightly different across conditions (congruent: 4.75, incongruent: 5.23, t(64) = 2.07, p < 0.05).

issues.description: All three experiments recruited undergraduate students from Royal Holloway, University of London, with no mention of whether participants were excluded if they had participated in a prior experiment. Experiment 3 used stimuli directly drawn from Experiment 1's nonword set ('Eighty experimental nonwords... were selected from Experiment 1'). Prior exposure to these specific stimuli would constitute non-naivety, potentially inflating or distorting effects in Experiment 3 through explicit memory of category judgements made in Experiment 1.
issues.quote: Eighty experimental nonwords with suffix spellings diagnostic for adjectives (10 suffixes) or nouns (10 suffixes) were selected from Experiment 1.

issues.description: The eye-tracking experiment used a viewing distance of 140 cm, far outside the standard range of 60–80 cm used in reading research. At 140 cm with 14pt Courier font (stated as 0.3°/character), characters subtend a very small visual angle, creating an atypical reading situation. This is rarely used in sentence reading paradigms, may require abnormal saccadic behaviour, and reduces comparability with the established literature cited. No justification is given for this choice.
issues.quote: Participants were seated at a viewing distance of 140cm, with this position maintained with a table-mounted head and chin rest.

issues.description: Participants in Experiment 3 were explicitly warned that every sentence would contain a nonword. This forewarning likely induces a metalinguistic processing strategy in which participants actively scan for and evaluate the novel word rather than reading naturally. The effects observed (regressions-out, go-past elevation) may therefore reflect deliberate strategic processing rather than the automatic sensitivity to spelling-meaning regularities that the authors claim to demonstrate.
issues.quote: Participants were warned that each sentence would contain a nonword and were asked to read for comprehension.

issues.description: Throughout the paper, lexical category (noun, verb, adjective) is treated as equivalent to 'meaning.' However, lexical category is a grammatical/syntactic feature, not a semantic one. The paper acknowledges this is a specific operationalisation by citing Baayen et al. (2011) but does not adequately justify why grammatical category constitutes 'meaning' in the sense relevant to theories of reading and word recognition. This conflation also means the constructs 'diagnosticity' and 'specificity' measure spelling-to-grammar relationships, not spelling-to-meaning relationships as claimed in the title and abstract.
issues.quote: This paper focuses on one aspect of word meaning, specifically, lexical category (e.g., noun, adjective, verb; see Baayen et al., 2011, for a similar conceptualisation of "meaning").

issues.description: In Experiment 1, participants make explicit adjective-versus-noun judgements about nonwords in a labelled forced-choice task with formal grammatical category definitions on screen. This taps conscious, metalinguistic knowledge rather than the implicit statistical sensitivity claimed throughout. The authors acknowledge in the general discussion that knowledge was 'acquired through implicit statistical learning processes,' but the primary evidence (Experiment 1) uses an entirely explicit paradigm. The construct being measured and the construct claimed are mismatched.
issues.quote: Participants were seated in a quiet room and read the following instructions: 'You will be asked to decide if a letter string looks like a noun or an adjective. NOUN is a person, animal, place, thing, or idea... ADJECTIVE is an attribute of a noun'

issues.description: The diagnosticity and specificity of suffix spellings are correlated with how common those spellings are in the lexicon. More frequent suffix spellings (e.g., -ness, -ity) are also highly diagnostic. Participants' behavioural responses may therefore reflect frequency-based orthographic familiarity rather than sensitivity to spelling-to-category mappings. The authors partially address this by showing token-based measures fit less well, but they do not include orthographic type or token frequency as a covariate in the regression models to partial out this alternative explanation.
issues.quote: More diagnostic suffixes were more likely to be ascribed to the category that they denote... we find no relationship between token frequency and diagnosticity.

issues.description: The paper repeatedly claims English spelling 'evolved' or 'has become fractionated' to 'maximise the transmission of meaningful information.' This is a teleological claim that implies directionality and purpose in a historical process. The synchronic computational data presented here cannot establish evolutionary directionality; the diachronic support cited (Berg & Aronoff, 2017) is limited to a few suffixes. Crucially, the alternative hypothesis—that the current state of spelling-meaning alignment is an incidental consequence of other spelling-sound changes, not a functionally optimised outcome—is not considered.
issues.quote: English spelling may have become fractionated in such a way that the high degree of spelling-sound inconsistency maximises the transmission of meaningful information... the multiple spellings permissible for particular sound sequences seem to be fractionated in such a way as to allow particular spellings to become reserved for particular functions.

issues.description: The computational analysis considers only three lexical categories: nouns, adjectives, and verbs. Adverbs—which have a large, coherent suffix class (-LY, -WARD, -WAYS, -WISE)—are excluded entirely. In Appendix A, -LY has Diagnosticity_A = 0.039, N = 0.006, V = 0.002, summing to only 0.047, indicating that ~95% of -LY words are coded as belonging to none of the three included categories (because they are adverbs). This exclusion artificially lowers the apparent entropy and raises apparent diagnosticity of other suffixes by removing a major competing category, inflating the reported regularity of the writing system.
issues.quote: Our analyses consider three major lexical categories: nouns, adjectives, and verbs.

issues.description: The authors use 'feedforward' to mean spelling-to-meaning mappings and 'feedback' to mean meaning-to-spelling mappings. In the established psycholinguistics and cognitive neuroscience literature, feedforward and feedback refer to bottom-up (stimulus-driven) versus top-down (knowledge-driven) processing flows within a system. Using these terms with entirely different meanings without explicit redefinition creates conceptual confusion and may mislead readers familiar with the standard usage.
issues.quote: In this paper, we focus solely on what is usually referred to as 'feedforward' effects. That is, we hypothesise that diagnosticity, a measure of spelling-to-meaning consistency, would impact on tasks that involve the production of spelling, while specificity... would impact on tasks involving the mapping of print to meaning

issues.description: For all three experiments, participant descriptions are limited to 'undergraduate students.' No information is reported on age range, sex distribution, handedness, whether participants were native English speakers, years of education, or reading ability. Given that the study directly concerns sensitivity to English-specific orthographic regularities, native language in particular is critical: non-native speakers might show very different patterns for reasons having nothing to do with the theoretical claims.
issues.quote: Participants were 46 undergraduate students at Royal Holloway, University of London.

issues.description: No effect sizes (Cohen's d, partial η², odds ratios, or similar) are reported for any of the three experiments. Given the focus on graded relationships between corpus statistics and behaviour, effect size estimates are essential for interpreting the practical magnitude of the claimed regularities and for future meta-analyses or power calculations.
issues.quote: Results showed a main effect of suffix condition such that noun-diagnostic suffixes elicited more "noun" responses (B = -1.57, z = -4.224, p < 0.0001)

issues.description: While Experiments 1 and 2 provide a model formula, this specifies only random intercepts for subjects with no random slopes. Experiment 3 is described verbally as including 'random intercepts for subjects and for suffixes' but no model formula is given, and no information about random slope structure, convergence behavior (except for one refitted model), or model comparison criteria (AIC/BIC) is reported. The full model output is relegated to OSF without summary here, preventing evaluation of the models' adequacy.
issues.quote: All models included trial order as a main effect, and random intercepts for subjects and for suffixes. However, in the interest of space we report only those effects pertaining to our main variable of interest, congruency.

issues.description: The sentence contexts in Experiments 2 and 3 were constructed by the authors to suggest noun, adjective, or verb interpretations. No norming study was conducted to verify that (a) the intended category interpretation was reliably perceived, (b) sentences were equally plausible and natural across conditions, or (c) no orthographic or phonological properties of the nonwords interacted with context type. Without this, it is unknown whether participants' responses reflected suffix spelling knowledge or simply response to contextual plausibility.
issues.quote: Sixty-six sentences were designed following one of three possible context templates (noun, adjective, or verb template)

issues.description: Experiment 1 reports that 11.7% of data points are missing due to timeouts or non-response button presses, yet the analysis proceeds without describing how these missing data were handled. Complete case analysis (exclusion of missing trials) is implied but not stated. No analysis is reported of whether missing data were randomly distributed across suffix types, diagnosticity levels, or participants. Systematic missingness (e.g., participants timing out more on harder, less diagnostic suffixes) would bias the diagnosticity effect estimates.
issues.quote: We used generalised mixed modelling analysis from the lme4 package in R (Bates et al., 2014) on 1,625 data points (11.7% of data points were missing due to timeouts or button presses that did not correspond to a response).

issues.description: The entire computational analysis relies on CELEX (Baayen et al., 1993), a database compiled in 1993. The authors motivate derivational suffixation by noting its role in labelling new concepts ('Trumpists', 'Brexiteers'), yet the very database used cannot contain such words. CELEX is also known to lack coverage of many technical, informal, and borrowed words that have entered English since the early 1990s. More current databases (e.g., SUBTLEX-UK, BNC2014, or English Lexicon Project) could change the diagnosticity and specificity estimates materially.
issues.quote: We extracted all single-word entries from the CELEX database (Baayen, Piepenbrock & van Rijn, 1993)

issues.description: In the General Discussion, the authors assert that 'diagnosticity and specificity are characteristic not of the English writing system exclusively but rather reflect general cognitive principles and thus must manifest, in one way or another, in other orthographies.' This strong universalist claim is entirely speculative and not tested. It contradicts the authors' own acknowledgement that English spelling evolved 'under minimal environmental constraints (unlike French and Italian).' The claim is presented as plausible conjecture but is phrased in sufficiently confident language ('must manifest') to constitute an overclaim.
issues.quote: It is our view that diagnosticity and specificity are characteristic not of the English writing system exclusively but rather reflect general cognitive principles and thus must manifest, in one way or another, in other orthographies.

issues.description: No power analysis is reported for any of the three experiments. Sample sizes of N = 46, 29, and 47 are relatively modest for mixed-effects designs with graded continuous predictors (diagnosticity and specificity) that require adequate power to detect interaction effects. Experiment 2 is particularly underpowered with only 29 participants and 11 suffix conditions, and the token-based specificity interaction failed to replicate in that experiment. Power considerations are especially important given the exploratory nature of Experiment 3.
issues.quote: Participants were 29 undergraduate students from Royal Holloway University of London. Sampling conditions were otherwise the same as in Experiment 1.

issues.description: In Experiment 1, the authors report that 'adjective-specific suffixes did not show an effect of diagnosticity (p > 0.8)' for token measures, while noun-diagnostic suffixes did (p < 0.05). This asymmetry between type and token analyses is noted without substantive explanation ('The results based on token measures were similar... but adjective-specific suffixes did not show an effect of diagnosticity'). The authors conclude that token measures provide a 'poorer fit' generally, but the selective failure for adjective suffixes specifically—not for noun suffixes—could indicate a ceiling or floor effect, a confound with token frequency, or a spurious type-based result. This selective pattern is not adequately addressed.
issues.quote: The results based on token measures were similar (main effect of diagnosticity, and an effect of diagnosticity on noun-diagnostic suffixes), but adjective-specific suffixes did not show an effect of diagnosticity (p > 0.8).
